newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek socialists face strong poll challenge.
newsitem.headline: Greek socialists face strong poll challenge.

text.p: Greeks voted on Sunday in an election seen as a close-run contest between socialist premier Costas Simitis and his conservative challenger Miltiadis Evert.
Simitis, 60, strongly pro-European in contrast to his predecessor, the late Andreas Papandreou, called the snap election confident he was leading in public opinion polls.
But he has found himself neck and neck with the conservatives after a lacklustre campaign.
Evert, 57, who launched a strong campaign and did not shy away from issuing populist promises could well find himself the winner of this contest, pollsters said.
About 8.5 million Greeks are required to cast a mandatory vote at polling stations around the country, which opened at sunrise at 0413 GMT and will close at sunset at 1620 GMT.
The socialists, in their first national election without flamboyant founder Andreas Papandreou, who died earlier this year, are leading in public opinion polls but within the margin of error.
Polls showed unprecedented voter apathy and a turn to smaller parties, reflecting public indifference to both the personalities and issues of the campaign.

Past elections had been marked by contrast between the conservative pro-European stance and Papandreou's anti-European and anti-NATO policies. These emotional issues have paled with Simitis' decidedly pro-European line.
"Get off the couch!" was the front-page headline in the liberal Eleftherotypia newspaper on voting day.

With the European Union's specific prescription for turning around Greece's ailing ecomomy, parties have had little room to clash on most economic issues and have turned their campaign into a personality contest.
The socialists have painted the diminutive, academic Simitis as a pragmatic visionary able to lead Greece in a 21st century united Europe.

But his academic rhetoric, often accompanied by charts, failed to rouse the hard-core socialists used to Papandreou's more passionate style, which got him three landslide victories in 1981, 1985 and 1993.
Evert banked on Simitis' calls for more work and sacrifices so that Greece can catch up with its EU partners to lose the socialist votes. He promised rises in pensions and a relaxation in taxation.
But both parties' efforts to woo voters failed to register on public opinion polls, which showed about 20 percent of Greeks had not made up their minds a week before election day.
"It is too close to call. Everything about this election is new -- the leaders, the number of undecided voters, the general apathy," poll analyst Ilias Nikolakopoulos said on television.
